# 7. Observable representations and autonomous closure {#ch-observable-closure}

Suitable current observables can retain the information needed for prediction and support autonomous finite approximations. The chapter moves from information constraints and scoped approximation obstructions to a sufficient hierarchy and concrete initialized constructions. Its finite derivative and Gaussian calculations are developed together in [Mean-Field Peeling](02-gaussian-reuse.qmd#ch-gaussian-reuse).

## 5. The bounded-contraction closure class {#sec-docs-linear-dynamics-l908}

The negative result concerns identities on an open set of **all current
states**, uniformly in width. It does not impose a Gaussian initialization.
Use the normalized finite factors $\theta=(u,B,R,v)$ from ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l66]), and
write $\Theta_n$ for their full real vector space. The feature and
physical derivations are

$$
\mathscr D_n\text{ as in (2.1)},\qquad
\mathscr X_n=-2\kappa(f_n-y)\mathscr D_n.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l916}

A typed complete-contraction graph is a scalar tensor network made from
copies of $u,B,R,v$, with each layer index paired and summed. Tensor
slots retain their layer types, and a transpose reverses how the slots
are displayed, not the identity of the underlying tensor. Graphs are
identified by type- and slot-preserving isomorphisms; there are no isolated
index vertices. Let $P_G^{(n)}(\theta)$ be the contraction polynomial.
Its tensor degree is its number of tensor copies. The empty graph has
value one, and multiplication is disjoint union:

$$
P_G^{(n)}P_H^{(n)}=P_{G\sqcup H}^{(n)}.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l931}

For each fixed $D$, there are finitely many such graphs of degree at
most $D$: at most $2D$ typed slots must be paired in finitely many
ways among a finite list of tensor types. Denote this finite set by
$\mathcal G_D$.

Fix, independently of $n$, a spatial domain
$\mathcal O\subset\mathbb R^\nu$, a finite number $q$ of real scalar
fields, differential order $\sigma$, readout order $\rho$, degree
bound $D$, and finitely many readout points
$\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_s$. A boundary is allowed if coefficients and
the required derivatives extend smoothly to it. A **uniform
bounded-contraction encoder** has the form

$$
U_{\alpha,n}(\zeta;\theta)
 =\sum_{G\in\mathcal G_D}c_{\alpha,G,n}(\zeta)P_G^{(n)}(\theta),
\qquad 1\le\alpha\le q,
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l949}

where the coefficient functions are smooth and may depend on $n$.
Thus the same finite graph alphabet controls the whole spatial profile,
including all mixed derivatives, not just its values at the readout points.
Written in canonical weights, a graph with $a$ endpoint occurrences
acquires the factor $n^{-a/2}$ from ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l66]). Allowing width-dependent
coefficients makes ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l949]) exactly equivalent under that normalization.

A local differential-polynomial closure for a derivation
$\mathscr Y_n\in\{\mathscr D_n,\mathscr X_n\}$ consists of fixed
polynomials $F_\alpha$ in their finite jet arguments, with smooth fixed
spatial coefficients, and a fixed polynomial $G$, such that

$$
\mathscr Y_nU_{\alpha,n}(\zeta;\theta)
 =F_\alpha\!\left(\zeta,
 (\partial_\zeta^\beta U_{\gamma,n}(\zeta;\theta))_
 {1\le\gamma\le q,\ |\beta|\le\sigma}\right),
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l968}

$$
f_n(\theta)=G\!\left(
 (\partial_\zeta^\beta U_{\alpha,n}(\zeta_j;\theta))_
 {\alpha,j,\ |\beta|\le\rho}\right).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l976}

The expressions $F_\alpha,G$ are independent of width and state. The
identities are required, for every sufficiently large $n$, on a
nonempty open set in $\Theta_n$ and at every required spatial point.
For physical flow the fixed expressions may depend on the fixed label
and mobility.

In the analytic variant, the differential expressions and readout are
smooth in the spatial variables and real analytic in their finite jet
arguments on open domains containing their realized zero-network jet
tuples. The identities hold on a full state neighborhood of
$\theta=0$, with all compositions remaining in those domains. This
condition includes the actual basepoints
$(\partial^\beta U_{\alpha,n}(\zeta;0))$, which need not be zero
because of the empty-graph term. Smoothness here includes the mixed
derivatives used in finite prolongations.

::: {#thm-docs-linear-dynamics-l999}

### restricted scalar and PDE nonclosure

No encoder and
closure satisfying ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l949])--([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l976]) exists for $\mathscr D_n$, either in
the polynomial open-state class or in the analytic zero-neighborhood
class just specified. The same assertions hold for $\mathscr X_n$,
for every fixed $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\kappa>0$, including $y=0$.

In particular there is no fixed finite scalar list of bounded-degree
contractions with a polynomial autonomous ODE and polynomial output
readout in this state-universal sense. This is the case with no spatial
variables and zero differential/readout orders. It includes the usual
requirement that the first scalar coordinate itself be $f_n$; the
analytic statement uses the same zero-neighborhood condition.

The theorem allows arbitrary width-dependent encoder coefficients but
requires a width-uniform degree bound. It concerns local finite-order
differential expressions and finite-jet readouts. It asserts neither
nonclosure for arbitrary encoders nor nonclosure along only the single
Gaussian-initialized trajectory.

:::

### 6. Graph independence and the nonclosure proof {#sec-docs-linear-dynamics-l1018}

::: {#lem-docs-linear-dynamics-l1020}

### stable independence

Every fixed finite family of pairwise
nonisomorphic typed complete-contraction graphs has linearly independent
contraction polynomials for every sufficiently large width.

:::

[]{#proof-docs-linear-dynamics-l1024}

::: {.proof}
Treat all tensor entries as independent commuting
indeterminates. For this proof enlarge the graph class to typed incidence
networks in which an index vertex can have arbitrary valence. Take the
finite closure of the chosen graphs under all type-compatible quotients
of index vertices. For any network $H$ in that closure, let
$I_H^{(n)}$ be its injective contraction, in which distinct index
vertices of the same layer receive distinct indices. Partitioning all
index assignments by their equality relation gives

$$
P_G^{(n)}=\sum_\pi I_{G/\pi}^{(n)}.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1033}

The quotient may have index valence greater than two; this is precisely
why the auxiliary incidence networks are needed in ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1033]).

For width at least the number of vertices of each type in every network
under consideration, an injective labeling of one network produces a
tensor-entry monomial recording every tensor type and its incident typed
indices. It can occur in another injective contraction only when the
networks are isomorphic. Commutativity of entries forgets only the order
of identical tensor occurrences, already allowed by graph isomorphism.
There are no invisible isolated indices. Hence the injective contractions
of pairwise nonisomorphic auxiliary networks are linearly independent.

Suppose $\sum_Ga_GP_G^{(n)}=0$. Among graphs with $a_G\ne0$, choose
one with a maximal number of index vertices. Its discrete partition in
([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1033]) contributes $I_G$; a nontrivial quotient has fewer vertices, and
no graph with nonzero coefficient has more vertices. No other graph of
the same maximal size contributes this injective type. Its coefficient
cannot cancel, contradicting the preceding independence. Descending in
vertex count proves every $a_G=0$. $\square$

:::

This is a stable-width statement. At any one fixed width, sufficiently
large contraction families can satisfy dimension-specific identities.

To produce contractions of unbounded connected complexity, set

$$
A=RB,\qquad H=A^TA=B^TR^TRB.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1063}

Retain only endpoint differentiation in the feature derivation:
$\mathscr D_{0,n}v=Au$, $\mathscr D_{0,n}u=A^Tv$, and
$\mathscr D_{0,n}A=0$. For $j\ge0$, put

$$
U_j=v^TAH^ju,\qquad X_j=u^TH^{j+1}u,\qquad
Y_j=v^T(AA^T)^{j+1}v.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1072}

These $U_j$ are scalar auxiliary contractions, distinct from the
encoded fields with indices $\alpha,n$. The identities
$AH^jA^T=(AA^T)^{j+1}$ and
$(AA^T)^{j+1}A=AH^{j+1}$ give, by differentiating the two endpoints,

$$
\mathscr D_{0,n}U_j=X_j+Y_j,\qquad
\mathscr D_{0,n}X_j=\mathscr D_{0,n}Y_j=2U_{j+1}.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1083}

Since $U_0=f_n$, induction yields, for every integer $j\ge1$,

$$
\mathscr D_{0,n}^{2j-1}f_n
 =4^{j-1}\bigl[u^TH^ju+v^T(AA^T)^jv\bigr].
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1091}

Every tensor replacement in the full feature field ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l156]) is a sum of
monomials with coefficient $+1$. The product rule therefore gives
nonnegative coefficients for every contraction graph in every full
derivative of $f_n$. The endpoint-only differentiation histories in
([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1091]) are among those histories. Consequently

$$
\mathscr D_n^{2j-1}f_n\quad\text{has coefficient at least }4^{j-1}
\text{ on }\quad
\Gamma_j=u^T(B^TR^TRB)^ju.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1103}

Here $\Gamma_j$ also denotes its graph. It is a connected path of
tensor degree $4j+2$. These graph types are pairwise nonisomorphic.

Let $\mathcal S$ be the finite set of connected graph types occurring
in $\mathcal G_D$, and let

$$
\mathcal A_{\mathcal S}^{(n)}
 =\operatorname{span}\{P_H^{(n)}:
 \text{every connected component of }H\text{ lies in }\mathcal S\}.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1116}

This is a unital algebra by ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l931]). Every spatial derivative of ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l949]), of
arbitrarily high order, remains a linear combination of the same graphs,
since it differentiates only the coefficient functions. Thus every field
jet belongs to $\mathcal A_{\mathcal S}^{(n)}$.

We make explicit why a finite-order PDE forces all output time
derivatives into that same algebra. Introduce formal jet variables
$u_{\alpha,\beta}$, where $\beta$ is a spatial multi-index, and total
spatial derivatives

$$
D_i^{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\zeta_i}
 +\sum_{\alpha,\beta}u_{\alpha,\beta+e_i}
   \frac{\partial}{\partial u_{\alpha,\beta}},\qquad
D_{\mathrm{tot}}^\beta=\prod_i(D_i^{\mathrm{tot}})^{\beta_i}.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1133}

Here $e_i$ is the spatial multi-index unit vector. Each expression
involves finitely many jets, so only finitely many summands act on it.
Use independent jet copies at the finitely many readout points and define
the evolutionary derivative of a differential expression $J$ by

$$
\mathbf T_FJ=\sum_{j,\alpha,\beta}
 \frac{\partial J}{\partial u_{\alpha,\beta}^{(j)}}
 (D_{\mathrm{tot}}^\beta F_\alpha)(\zeta_j,u^{(j)}).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1146}

The state derivation and spatial derivatives commute because they act on
different variables. The chain rule and ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l968]) consequently imply

$$
\mathscr Y_nJ(j^\infty U_n)
 =(\mathbf T_FJ)(j^\infty U_n),\qquad
\mathscr Y_n^kf_n=(\mathbf T_F^kG)(j^\infty U_n).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1156}

The symbol $j^\infty U_n$ means substitution of the entire spatial jet;
each finite expression uses only finitely many of its entries.
For fixed $k$ only jets through order at most $\rho+k\sigma$ occur.
In the polynomial case the last expression is a finite polynomial in
those jets and belongs to $\mathcal A_{\mathcal S}^{(n)}$.

First take $\mathscr Y_n=\mathscr D_n$. Choose $j$ with
$4j+2>D$, so $\Gamma_j\notin\mathcal S$. Equation ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1156]) would
express $\mathscr D_n^{2j-1}f_n$ using graphs whose components all lie
in $\mathcal S$, while ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1103]) gives a positive coefficient of the
connected graph $\Gamma_j$. At this fixed iteration order only
finitely many graph types occur, uniformly in $n$, regardless of the
encoder coefficient values. @lem-docs-linear-dynamics-l1020 makes coefficient comparison valid
for sufficiently large $n$, a contradiction. If the starting identities
hold only on a nonempty open state set, each substituted identity is a
polynomial in the tensor entries. Such a polynomial vanishing on an open
set vanishes identically: restrict to coordinate lines through a small
open box and successively apply the fact that a one-variable polynomial
with an interval of zeros is zero. Thus the same argument applies.

For the analytic case, scale all four factors by a common scalar
$\lambda$ and recenter each field jet at its actual zero-state value:

$$
\partial^\beta U_{\alpha,n}(\zeta;\lambda\theta)
 -\partial^\beta U_{\alpha,n}(\zeta;0).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1186}

Every nonzero centered jet has positive $\lambda$-order. At any fixed
power $\lambda^N$, only finitely many monomials in the Taylor
expansion of a composed finite-jet expression can contribute. Each such
coefficient is a product of graph coefficients from ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l949]), and so has
components only in $\mathcal S$. The smooth mixed derivatives stipulated
above justify finite spatial prolongations and extraction of these Taylor
coefficients. All expansions are at realized zero-state tuples within
the specified analytic domains.

The cubic feature vector field raises homogeneous tensor degree by two.
Thus $\mathscr D_n^{2j-1}f_n$ is homogeneous of degree $4j+2$.
Comparing that power of $\lambda$ in ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1156]) gives the same contradiction
with ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1103]). This proves the feature-flow assertions, including scalar
closures as a special case.

For physical flow with $y\ne0$, decompose

$$
\mathscr X_n=2\kappa y\mathscr D_n-2\kappa f_n\mathscr D_n.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1209}

The first summand raises tensor degree by two and the second by six.
Therefore the lowest-degree homogeneous component of
$\mathscr X_n^kf_n$ is exactly

$$
(2\kappa y)^k\mathscr D_n^kf_n.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1218}

Choosing $k=2j-1$ again gives a nonzero $\Gamma_j$ coefficient in
that homogeneous component. Both the polynomial identity argument and
the analytic Taylor argument contradict ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1156]) degree by degree.

For $y=0$, define homogeneous polynomials $P_k$ by

$$
\mathscr X_n^kf_n=(-2\kappa)^kP_k,\qquad
P_0=f_n,\qquad P_{k+1}=f_n\mathscr D_nP_k.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1229}

Every graph coefficient in $P_k$ is nonnegative. Induction shows it
contains $f_n^k\mathscr D_n^kf_n$ with positive coefficient: applying
$f_n\mathscr D_n$ to that term produces
$f_n^{k+1}\mathscr D_n^{k+1}f_n$, and every other contribution is
nonnegative. At $k=2j-1$ this includes a graph with $k$ components
equal to the output path and one component $\Gamma_j$. No product of
graphs from $\mathcal S$ can supply that last component. The polynomial
has homogeneous degree $4+6k$, so coefficient comparison at that
degree works in both classes. @lem-docs-linear-dynamics-l1020 again gives a contradiction. This
completes @thm-docs-linear-dynamics-l999 for every label. The stationary initialized
population at $y=0$ is consistent with this result, which quantifies
over an open set of current states. $\square$

### 7. What unrestricted fields can encode {#sec-docs-linear-dynamics-l1248}

Field count alone cannot imply the preceding obstruction. An exact
one-field transport construction illustrates the missing encoder
restriction without invoking a width limit.

Let $\Phi_n^s$ denote the local feature flow ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l156]). Define the germ at
$s=0$ of the output profile of a current state by

$$
E_n(\theta)(s)=f_n(\Phi_n^s\theta).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1257}

The flow property gives, wherever the times are defined,

$$
U_n(\tau,s)=E_n(\Phi_n^\tau\theta)(s)=f_n(\Phi_n^{\tau+s}\theta),\qquad
\partial_\tau U_n=\partial_sU_n,\qquad
U_n(\tau,0)=f_n(\Phi_n^\tau\theta).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1264}

There is a common local interval on a common operator-norm neighborhood,
independent of width. For $\|\mathcal C(0)\|\le\varepsilon$,
$\varepsilon>0$, on the $2\varepsilon$-ball the feature field
$(\mathcal C^T)^3$ is bounded by $8\varepsilon^3$ and Lipschitz
with constant $12\varepsilon^2$, by telescoping. On
$|s|\le(24\varepsilon^2)^{-1}$, the Picard integral map has contraction
constant at most $1/2$ and image norm at most
$\varepsilon+\varepsilon/3<2\varepsilon$. Thus ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1257]) is a
state-universal local output realization. Repeated chain rules give

$$
\partial_s^kE_n(\theta)(0)=\mathscr D_n^kf_n(\theta).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1281}

Its $(2j-1)$-st jet contains $\Gamma_j$. It cannot satisfy ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l949]),
even though the PDE is linear, first order, and uses one scalar field
and one spatial variable. This is a local statement for feature flow;
feature-time completeness is not needed or asserted.

For physical flow the construction is global on a fixed spatial domain.
Let $\Psi_n^t$ be the global finite-width flow for arbitrary initial
states, proved by ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l655]). Define

$$
\widehat E_n(\theta)(s)=f_n(\Psi_n^s\theta),\quad s\ge0,\qquad
(S_tu)(s)=u(s+t).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1295}

On $C([0,\infty))$ with the topology of uniform convergence on compact
intervals, $S_t$ is a continuous forward semigroup. For a compact
interval in $s$, uniform continuity on a slightly larger interval
proves continuity in $t$, and
$\sup_{s\le S}|S_tu-S_tv|\le\sup_{s\le S+t}|u-v|$ proves
continuity in the profile. Its output profiles satisfy

$$
\widehat E_n(\Psi_n^t\theta)=S_t\widehat E_n(\theta),\qquad
\partial_tU=\partial_sU,\qquad U(t,0)=f_n(\Psi_n^t\theta).
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1308}

For $C^1$ initial profiles this PDE has the unique classical solution
$U(t,s)=U(0,t+s)$. Along the characteristic
$\tau\mapsto(t-\tau,s+\tau)$, its derivative is
$-U_t+U_s=0$, proving the formula and uniqueness; no inflow boundary
datum at $s=0$ is required. Continuous profiles give the same unique
translation evolution in the semigroup sense. Hence ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1308]) is an
autonomous, restartable, global forward output realization on a fixed
domain for every width and current state.

This encoder uses the whole future output trajectory to initialize its
profile. It is an exact counterexample to an unrestricted prohibition of
PDE output realizations, not a method for constructing the population
from its Gaussian source. The population ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l96]) has that additional
constructive content, established by Sections [2](09-trainability.qmd#sec-docs-linear-dynamics-l151)--[4](09-trainability.qmd#sec-docs-linear-dynamics-l735).

Two finite checks further delimit elementary compression claims. At
width one, the normalized states

$$
(v,R,B,u)=(1,1,1,1),\qquad (2,1,1,\tfrac12)
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1332}

have the same output and cyclic characteristic polynomial
$\lambda^4-1$. Formula ([-@eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l77]) gives kernels $4$ and $25/4$,
respectively. Thus the cyclic eigenvalues alone do not determine the
instantaneous feature derivative, or the physical derivative when
$y\ne1$. At that same fixed width a polynomial
scalar closure does exist: with $a=v^2,b=R^2,c=B^2,d_0=u^2$,

$$
\mathscr D_1a=\mathscr D_1b=\mathscr D_1c=\mathscr D_1d_0=2f_1,
\qquad
\mathscr D_1f_1=bcd_0+acd_0+abd_0+abc.
$$ {#eq-docs-linear-dynamics-l1344}

These follow by differentiating the four scalar factors. Multiplication
by $-2\kappa(f_1-y)$ gives a physical scalar closure as well.
This confirms why @thm-docs-linear-dynamics-l999 requires identities for all sufficiently
large widths. Neither this example nor the transport profile is a
bounded-contraction closure in that theorem's width-uniform class.

## Literal storage of a frozen-top neural tangent hierarchy {#sec-nth-storage}

The preceding encoding obstruction depends on the permitted representation.
Here that representation is fixed explicitly: ordered neural tangent hierarchy
(NTH) tensors, retained as literal arrays and truncated by freezing their
highest rank. This rule, associated with the NTH of @huang2020nth, is considered
in the book's feature-learning metric with zero initial readout. No theorem
for another parameterization or readout initialization is transferred.
On a correlated growing dataset, the necessary and sufficient retained size
is $\exp[\Theta(\log m\log n)]$ on a fixed short physical interval.

### Model, closure, and storage {#sec-nth-storage-setup}

There are $m\ge1$ deterministic samples, independent of initialization,
$v_a=x_a/\sqrt d\in\mathbb R^d$, with $\|v_a\|_2\le1$ and $|y_a|\le1$.
Predictions indexed by $v$ mean the physical network input $x=\sqrt d\,v$.
The two hidden activations are identity. In canonical layer notation,
$W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, $W^{(2)}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$,
$W^{(3)}\in\mathbb R^n$, and
$$
h^{(1)}=W^{(1)}v,\quad h^{(2)}=W^{(2)}h^{(1)},\quad
f_n(v)=\frac{W^{(3)\top}h^{(2)}}n,\qquad
r_a=f_n(v_a)-y_a,\quad \mathcal L=\frac1{2m}\sum_a r_a^2.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-network}
Initially the first two matrices have independent entries with laws
$\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $\mathcal N(0,1/n)$, respectively, and $W^{(3)}(0)=0$.
All blocks train with mobilities $(n,1,n)$. The half-MSE is deliberate:
the book's full-MSE flow at physical time $t$ equals this flow at time $2t$.
Thus the interval below becomes $[0,T/2]$ under full-MSE.

Put
$$
B=W^{(1)}/\sqrt n,\qquad W=W^{(2)},\qquad c=W^{(3)}/\sqrt n,
\qquad \theta=(B,W,c).
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-normalization}
Then $f_n(v)=c^\top WBv$ and training is ordinary Euclidean/Frobenius
gradient flow in $\theta$. In particular $B_0,W_0$ have independent
$\mathcal N(0,1/n)$ entries. Define the fixed data summaries and evolving
prediction coefficient by
$$
Q=\frac1m\sum_a v_av_a^\top,\qquad b=\frac1m\sum_a y_av_a,\qquad
w=B^\top W^\top c,\qquad f_n(v)=v^\top w.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-data}
Here $\|Q\|_{\rm op}\le1$, $\|b\|_2\le1$, and the exact dense equations are
$$
\dot B=W^\top c(b-Qw)^\top,\qquad
\dot W=c[B(b-Qw)]^\top,\qquad \dot c=WB(b-Qw).
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-dense}

For arbitrary input vectors define the source field and ordered tensors by
$$
\begin{aligned}
V(v;\theta)&=\nabla_\theta f_n(v)
 =(W^\top cv^\top,\ c(Bv)^\top,\ WBv),\\
K_1(v;\theta)&=f_n(v),\\
K_{r+1}(v_0,\ldots,v_r;\theta)
 &=D_\theta K_r(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1};\theta)[V(v_r;\theta)].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-source}
Every input slot is linear; permutation symmetry is not assumed.
$K_r(\mathbf v;0)$ means evaluation at $\theta_0$.
For an integer $q\ge2$, copy these initialized tensors through rank $q$,
freeze rank $q$, and evolve all lower ranks by
$$
\dot K_r^{(q)}(\mathbf v;t)
 =-\frac1m\sum_a r_a^{(q)}(t)K_{r+1}^{(q)}(\mathbf v,v_a;t),
\quad r_a^{(q)}=f_{n,q}(v_a)-y_a,\quad f_{n,q}(v)=K_1^{(q)}(v).
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-closure}
The closure uses its own residual. In each array the first slot is a training
input or a passive coordinate query $e_i$, $1\le i\le d$; all later slots
are training indices. Passive queries have no labels. Linearity gives the
exact decoder $f_{n,q}(t,v)=v^\top w_q(t)$ for any later query, where
$w_q(t)=(f_{n,q}(t,e_i))_{i=1}^d$.
The moving and frozen array counts are, respectively,
$$
N_{\rm mov}(q)=(m+d)\sum_{r=1}^{q-1}m^{r-1},\qquad
N_{\rm top}(q)=(m+d)m^{q-1},\qquad N_{\rm arr}=N_{\rm mov}+N_{\rm top}.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-counts}
The dataset adds at most $md+m$ fixed scalars. These are retained real
coordinates, excluding coefficient-generation work, initialization peak
memory, numerical integration and bit precision. They do not charge a
factorized or implicit encoding. Once the initial tensors have been formed
from $B_0,W_0$ and the data, those dense matrices need not be retained.

Fix throughout
$$
T=2^{-15},\qquad
E_n(q)=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}|f_n(t,v)-f_{n,q}(t,v)|,\qquad
D_n=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}|f_n(t,v)-\widetilde f_n(t,v)|,
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-errors}
where $\widetilde f_n$ is an independent dense initialization on the same
dataset. Both errors use the same physical window and sphere.
In probability statements, nonexistence on the window counts as failure;
$E_n(q)\le A D_n$ includes $E_n(q)=D_n=0$ without taking a ratio.

::: {#thm-nth-storage-matching}
### Matched literal storage

Fix $0<Y\le1$, a success probability $0<p<1$, and an accuracy factor $A>0$.
For $4\mid m$, $4\le m\le\sqrt n$, take $d=m+1$, orthonormal coordinates
$e_0,\ldots,e_m$, and
$$
v_a=\frac{e_0+e_a}{\sqrt2},\qquad
y_a=Ys_a,\qquad
s_a=\begin{cases}1,&a\le3m/4,\\-1,&a>3m/4.\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-hard-data}
Let $S_n(p,A)$ be the minimum of $N_{\rm arr}(q)+md+m$ over deterministic
orders $q\ge2$ for which $\Pr\{E_n(q)\le A D_n\}\ge p$.
For sufficiently large $n$, uniformly over the displayed sample range,
$$
\exp[c_Y\log m\log n]\ \le S_n(p,A)
\le\exp[C_Y\log m\log n]
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-matched}
for positive constants depending only on $Y$; the width threshold may also
depend on $p,A$. The same order holds for the minimum moving-array count,
and survives omission of a zero odd frozen top.
The lower bound excludes all insufficient orders simultaneously, including
initialization-dependent order selection under a deterministic budget.
For $m=4\lfloor n^a/4\rfloor$, fixed $0<a\le1/2$, the size is
$\exp[\Theta_{Y,a}((\log n)^2)]$.
:::

::: {#cor-nth-storage-general-upper}
### A uniform local upper bound for deterministic datasets

For every dataset in the setup, $n\ge4$ and $1\le d\le n$, put
$$
q_n=\left\lceil\frac{\log(2^{37}n^3)}{\log1024}\right\rceil,\qquad
c_*=4-\tfrac32\log9>0.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-order}
With probability at least $1-4e/\sqrt n-4e^{-c_*n}$, the dense and
order-$q_n$ solutions exist and $E_n(q_n)\le D_n/n$.
For $m\ge2$ their arrays satisfy
$N_{\rm mov}\le2(m+d)m^{q_n-2}$ and
$N_{\rm arr}\le2(m+d)m^{q_n-1}$; for $m=1$ the exact counts are
$(1+d)(q_n-1)$ moving and $1+d$ frozen.
No Gram gap or positive label mean is required. If $b=0$, both dense
predictors and the closure vanish identically.
The probability is for each deterministic dataset, not one simultaneous
anti-concentration event for all datasets.
:::

The proof separates three issues. Ordered source integration controls the
unchanged closure with its own residual. A nonzero omitted derivative and
analytic continuation force a lower error at every finite order.
Upper and lower probability bounds on the *actual* dense-pair discrepancy
then give the two storage inequalities.

::: {#lem-nth-storage-source-control}
### Ordered source convergence and a common analytic disk

Suppose deterministically that $\|B_0\|_{\rm op},\|W_0\|_{\rm op}\le4$.
The dense solution and every finite closure exist on $[0,T]$.
Their prediction coefficients extend holomorphically to $|t|<R_0=2^{-12}$,
with norms at most one there; the dense coefficient satisfies
$\|w(t)\|_2\le\|b\|_2(e^{1875|t|}-1)<\|b\|_2$ when $b\ne0$.
Simultaneously for every $q\ge2$, with $j=2\lfloor q/2\rfloor+1$,
$$
E_n(q)\le64(j+1)(j+2)(\|b\|_2/4096)^j
\le64\|b\|_2\,1024^{-q}.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-geometric}
:::

[]{#proof-nth-storage-source-control}

::: {.proof}
In the maximum block norm, a source derivative replaces one of the three
parameter leaves of $c^\top WBv_0$ by a quadratic expression.
After $k$ derivatives there are at most $(k+2)!/2$ terms, each with $k+3$
parameter leaves and one occurrence of each input. Products, transposes,
outer products and scalar contractions are bounded by their operator/vector
norm products; this construction introduces no free trace. Consequently,
on a block-norm ball of radius $s$,
$$
|K_{k+1}(v_0,\ldots,v_k;\theta)|
\le\tfrac12(k+2)!\,s^{k+3}\prod_i\|v_i\|_2,\qquad
|K_{k+1}(\mathbf v;0)|\le32\,4^k(k+2)!\prod_i\|v_i\|_2.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-leaf-bound}
Readout reflection $J(B,W,c)=(B,W,-c)$ obeys $f_n\circ J=-f_n$ and
$V(v;J\theta)=-JV(v;\theta)$. Induction gives
$K_r(\mathbf v;J\theta)=(-1)^rK_r(\mathbf v;\theta)$.
Thus all odd initialized ranks vanish.

Extend @eq-nth-storage-dense over complex coordinates using ordinary
transposes. Within distance one of $\theta_0$, all block norms are at most
five, $\|w\|_2\le125$, and $\|b-Qw\|_2\le126$.
Each block velocity is at most $25\cdot126=3150$.
A unit variation changes $w$ by at most $75$, so each velocity derivative
is at most $5\cdot126+5\cdot126+25\cdot75=3135$.
Picard integration on $|t|\le R_0$ maps this path ball into itself and
contracts, since $3150R_0,3135R_0<1$. Its uniform iterates give a
holomorphic solution, unique also as a real polynomial ODE solution.
Differentiating $w=B^\top W^\top c$ gives
$\|w'\|_2\le1875(\|b\|_2+\|w\|_2)$.
Integration along a radial segment and scalar Gronwall give the stated bound,
using $1875R_0<\log2$.

For a vector path $z$, put $a_z(t)=b-Qz(t)$. Define a vector-valued map by
its pairing with every $v$:
$$
v^\top\mathcal F_q[z](t)=
\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}\int_{0<s_k<\cdots<s_1<t}
K_{k+1}(v,a_z(s_1),\ldots,a_z(s_k);0)\,ds_k\cdots ds_1.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-ordered-map}
The complex integrals follow the straight segment to $t$;
$\mathcal F_\infty$ uses all $k\ge1$.
The first appended slot is always at the latest integration time.
For $u_a(t)=(y_a-v_a^\top z(t))/m$, define
$I_{a_1\ldots a_k}[u]$ as the ordered integral of
$\prod_i u_{a_i}(s_i)$ over that simplex, and $I_\varnothing=1$.
For each retained rank the exact reconstruction is
$$
K_r^{(q)}(\mathbf v;t)=
\sum_{k=0}^{q-r}\ \sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_k}
K_{r+k}(\mathbf v,v_{a_1},\ldots,v_{a_k};0)
I_{a_1\ldots a_k}[u](t).
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-reconstruction}
Differentiating the outer integration limit gives
@eq-nth-storage-closure whenever $z=\mathcal F_q[z]$; multilinearity
identifies its rank-one equation with @eq-nth-storage-ordered-map.
Thus a fixed point supplies all actual arrays, their initialized values,
and their frozen top. Polynomial ODE uniqueness identifies this solution
with the prescribed closure.

On the unit ball of holomorphic coefficient paths on $|t|\le R_0$,
$\|a_z\|\le2$. The simplex volume and @eq-nth-storage-leaf-bound bound
every finite map by $32\sum_{k\ge1}(k+1)(k+2)(8R_0)^k<0.38$.
Telescoping its $k$ source slots bounds its Lipschitz constant by
$16\sum_{k\ge1}k(k+1)(k+2)(8R_0)^k<0.2$.
Contraction gives all the asserted analytic closure paths.

On real $[0,T]$, if $\|b\|_2>0$, use instead the path ball of radius
$\|b\|_2$ and put $x=8T=1/4096$. Uniformly over finite and infinite maps,
$$
\|\mathcal F_q[z]\|_\infty
\le64\|b\|_2[(1-x)^{-3}-1]<\|b\|_2/16,\qquad
L\le\frac{96x}{(1-x)^4}<\frac1{32}.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-contraction}
These follow from $\|a_z\|\le2\|b\|_2$ and
$\|a_z-a_{\widetilde z}\|\le\|z-\widetilde z\|$; the series converge
uniformly. The dense path is the infinite fixed point: repeated integration
of its exact hierarchy leaves, after $N$ steps, an $N$-fold integral of
$K_{N+1}(v,a_w(s_1),\ldots,a_w(s_N);\theta(s_N))$.
Previously selected source vectors are held fixed during each integration.
By the dense bound and @eq-nth-storage-leaf-bound, this remainder is at most
$\frac{125}{2}(N+1)(N+2)(10\|b\|_2T)^N$, which tends to zero.

Parity makes $j=2\lfloor q/2\rfloor+1$ the first possible omitted index.
For $z_0=x\|b\|_2$, the omitted tail is at most
$$
32\sum_{k\ge j}(k+1)(k+2)z_0^k
\le32(j+1)(j+2)z_0^j\frac{1+z_0}{(1-z_0)^3}.
$$
Here $(j+\ell+1)(j+\ell+2)\le(j+1)(j+2)(\ell+1)^2$ and
$\sum_{\ell\ge0}(\ell+1)^2z^\ell=(1+z)/(1-z)^3$.
The difference of the two own-residual fixed points is bounded by this
tail divided by $1-L$. Since $(1+x)/[(1-x)^3(1-L)]<2$ and
$(j+1)(j+2)\le4^j$ for $j\ge2$, @eq-nth-storage-geometric follows.
If $b=0$, the dense initial state is stationary and the zero path is a
fixed point of every finite map; uniqueness proves the omitted case.
:::

::: {#lem-nth-storage-gaussian-control}
### Gaussian events and dense concentration

For $d\le n$ the matrix-norm event in @lem-nth-storage-source-control has
probability at least $1-2e^{-c_*n}$. For the hard family, with probability
at least $1-n^{-1}-Ce^{-cn}$,
$$
D_n\le C\sqrt{\frac{m+\log(en)}n}.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-dense-upper}
Here and below unspecified $c,C>0$ are absolute.
:::

[]{#proof-nth-storage-gaussian-control}

::: {.proof}
A maximal $1/4$-separated sphere set has at most $9^d$ elements by comparing
disjoint radius-$1/8$ balls with the radius-$9/8$ ball, and is a $1/4$ net.
It gives $\|M\|_{\rm op}\le(4/3)\max_v\|Mv\|_2$.
For a fixed unit $v$, $n\|B_0v\|_2^2$ is $\chi_n^2$.
The Gaussian integral gives $\mathbb E e^{t\chi_n^2}=(1-2t)^{-n/2}$.
Exponential Markov at $t=4/9$ yields
$\Pr(\|B_0v\|_2>3)\le e^{-4n}9^{n/2}$.
The net union bound proves the asserted $e^{-c_*n}$ failure for $B_0$;
the same calculation proves it for $W_0$.

We supply the Gaussian Lipschitz concentration used here.
For standard Gaussian measure $\gamma$ in any finite dimension define
$P_s h(x)=\mathbb E h(e^{-s}x+\sqrt{1-e^{-2s}}\,Z)$, $Z\sim\gamma$.
Write $\mathscr A=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}^2-x\cdot\nabla$.
For positive bounded smooth $h$ with bounded derivatives and bounded away
from zero, Gaussian integration by parts gives $\partial_sP_sh=\mathscr A P_sh$ and
$$
-\frac{d}{ds}\operatorname{Ent}_\gamma(P_sh)
=\mathbb E_\gamma\frac{|\nabla P_sh|^2}{P_sh},\qquad
\operatorname{Ent}_\gamma(h)=
\mathbb E_\gamma(h\log h)-\mathbb E_\gamma h\log\mathbb E_\gamma h.
$$
Indeed $\mathbb E_\gamma[u\mathscr A v]
=-\mathbb E_\gamma\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$, and $P_s$ preserves $\gamma$.
Since $\nabla P_sh=e^{-s}P_s\nabla h$, weighted Cauchy--Schwarz gives
$|\nabla P_sh|^2/P_sh\le e^{-2s}P_s(|\nabla h|^2/h)$.
As $s\to\infty$, bounded convergence gives $P_sh\to\mathbb E_\gamma h$
and entropy tending to zero. Integrating proves
$\operatorname{Ent}_\gamma(h)\le\frac12\mathbb E_\gamma(|\nabla h|^2/h)$.
For bounded smooth $L$-Lipschitz $F$, with $L>0$, substitute $h=e^{\lambda F}$.
With $\psi(\lambda)=\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda F}$ this gives
$\lambda\psi'(\lambda)-\psi(\lambda)\le\lambda^2L^2/2$.
Integrating $(\psi/\lambda)'$ from zero yields
$\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda(F-\mathbb EF)}\le\lambda^2L^2/2$.
Markov, optimized at $\lambda=s/L^2$, and the same argument for $-F$ give
$$
\Pr\{|F-\mathbb EF|\ge s\}\le2e^{-s^2/(2L^2)}.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-gaussian-tail}
For an arbitrary Lipschitz $F$, truncate its values and smooth by convolution,
preserving the Lipschitz bound. Pass first through smoothing and then
truncation by dominated convergence: $|F(x)|\le|F(0)|+L|x|$, whose
exponential is Gaussian-integrable. The case $L=0$ is constant.
This also justifies the preceding
smooth calculations by bounded approximations.

On the matrix-norm event, all real states have block norms at most five.
For two such trajectories, measure parameter differences by the sum of
Frobenius/vector norms. Their $w$ values differ by at most $25$ times this
sum. Expanding @eq-nth-storage-dense bounds each velocity difference by
$1255$ times the sum: the two direct-product differences each cost $630$
on distinct blocks, while the residual difference costs $625$ on each block.
Gronwall gives factor $e^{3765t}$ in the sum norm.
Therefore a fixed unit-query output at any $t\le T$ is
$L_T=50e^{4000T}$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean list of initial entries.
Each such scalar map extends from the good set by
$F(x)=\inf_{z\ {\rm good}}\{F(z)+L_T\|x-z\|_2\}$, with unchanged
values and Lipschitz constant. Apply @eq-nth-storage-gaussian-tail to
the variance-$1/n$ Gaussian entries. Two independent copies differ by
at most $2s$ except with probability $4e^{-ns^2/(2L_T^2)}$, since
their extension means agree.

The coefficient path has time Lipschitz constant at most
$3\cdot25\cdot3150<250000$. Take a $1/2$ sphere net with at most $5^d$
points and a time grid with $M=\lceil nT\rceil+1$ points and mesh at most
$1/n$. A linear functional's sphere norm is at most twice its net maximum.
For $s=L_T\sqrt{2\log(4\,5^dM/\delta)/n}$ a union bound and the time
Lipschitz estimate give $D_n\le4s+500000/n$, except with probability
$\delta+4e^{-c_*n}$. Set $\delta=1/n$, $d=m+1$ to obtain
@eq-nth-storage-dense-upper.
:::

::: {#lem-nth-storage-omitted-derivative}
### A nonzero omitted derivative at every effective order

For the hard family put $\bar v=m^{-1}\sum_a s_av_a$,
$\lambda=\|\bar v\|_2$, and $v_*=\bar v/\lambda$.
With probability at least $1-Ce^{-cn}$, simultaneously for every $q\ge2$,
the signed prediction difference
$g_q(t)=m^{-1}\sum_a s_a[f_n(t,v_a)-f_{n,q}(t,v_a)]$ satisfies
$$
g_q^{(k)}(0)=0\ (k<j),\qquad
g_q^{(j)}(0)\ge j!(Y/64)^j,\qquad j=2\lfloor q/2\rfloor+1.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-omitted-jet}
:::

[]{#proof-nth-storage-omitted-derivative}

::: {.proof}
Directly, $G=(v_a^\top v_b)_{a,b}=\frac12(I_m+\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top)$,
$\lambda^2=1/8+1/(2m)$, label RMS is $Y$, and label variance is
$3Y^2/4$. Identity activations preserve this population feature Gram.
For $\xi_0=B_0v_*$, the Gaussian norm ratios
$\|\xi_0\|_2^2$ and $\|W_0\xi_0\|_2^2/\|\xi_0\|_2^2$ are independent
$\chi_n^2/n$. Each is at least $3/4$ except with exponentially small
probability: Markov applied to $e^{-\chi_n^2/6}$ gives failure at most
$\exp[n/8-(n/2)\log(4/3)]$.
Intersecting with the matrix-norm event gives
$\|\xi_0\|_2^2,\|W_0\xi_0\|_2^2\ge1/2$.

An odd frozen top is zero, so its predictor equals that of the preceding
even top: for $h=2\lfloor q/2\rfloor$, parity gives
$\mathcal F_q=\mathcal F_h$. Put $e=w-w_h$ and $j=h+1$.
The first omitted index $h$ vanishes, so the ordered series gives
$$
v^\top(\mathcal F_\infty[w]-\mathcal F_h[w])(t)
=\frac{t^j}{j!}K_{j+1}(v,b,\ldots,b;0)+O(t^{j+1}).
$$
If $e(t)=O(t^\ell)$, telescoping source slots in the finite map gives
$\mathcal F_h[w]-\mathcal F_h[w_h]=O(t^{\ell+1})$: one slot contributes
$-Qe$, and there is at least one time integration.
Since $e(0)=0$, repeated substitution in the difference of the two
fixed-point equations proves $e=O(t^j)$; the finite-map difference is
then $O(t^{j+1})$. This proves both the vanishing derivatives and the
displayed leading coefficient, with the closure's own feedback retained.
Contracting $v=\bar v$ and using $b=Y\bar v$ gives exactly
$$
g_q^{(j)}(0)=Y^j K_{j+1}(\bar v,\ldots,\bar v;0).
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-feedback-jet}

For source ascent of $F=c^\top WB\bar v$, write $\xi=Bv_*$ and use the
source clock $\tau=\lambda s$. The exact equations are
$\xi'=W^\top c$, $W'=c\xi^\top$, $c'=W\xi$.
Their invariants $WW^\top-cc^\top=W_0W_0^\top$ and
$\|\xi\|_2^2-\|c\|_2^2=\|\xi_0\|_2^2$ imply
$$
c''=(\|\xi_0\|_2^2I+W_0W_0^\top)c+2\|c\|_2^2c,\qquad
c(0)=0,\quad c'(0)=W_0\xi_0.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-source-ascent}
Diagonalize the positive semidefinite matrix, choosing eigenvector signs
so that $a=W_0\xi_0$ is coordinatewise nonnegative.
The Taylor recurrence then has nonnegative coefficients. With
$A_0=\|\xi_0\|_2^2$, $H=\|a\|_2^2$, coefficientwise induction compares
$c$ from below with $a u$, where
$u''=A_0u+2Hu^3$, $u(0)=0$, $u'(0)=1$.
Indeed the linear term dominates $A_0a_i u$ in coordinate $i$, and
$\|c\|_2^2c_i$ dominates $H a_i u^3$ at every successive coefficient.
Since $A_0,H\ge1/2$, it also compares $u$ from below with
$2\tan(\tau/2)$, which solves $u''=\frac12u+\frac18u^3$
with the same initial values.
Writing $\tan z=\sum_{k\ge0}t_kz^{2k+1}$,
$(2k+1)t_k=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t_it_{k-1-i}$ for $k\ge1$, and $t_0=1$,
give $t_k\ge3^{-k}$ by induction. Hence
$u\ge\tau/(1-\tau^2/12)$ coefficientwise.
The degree-$j=2k+1$ coefficient of $c^\top W\xi=c^\top c'$ is at least
$H(k+1)^2\,12^{-k}\ge8^{-j}$.
Returning to $F$ and clock $s$ multiplies its $j$th derivative by
$\lambda^{j+1}$. Since $\lambda\ge2^{-3/2}$,
$K_{j+1}(\bar v,\ldots,\bar v;0)\ge j!\lambda^{j+1}8^{-j}
\ge j!64^{-j}$, proving the claim on one event for every order.
:::

::: {#lem-nth-storage-analytic-transfer}
### From an omitted derivative to error on a real interval

If $g$ is holomorphic on a neighborhood of $|t|\le R$, bounded there by
two, and $|g^{(j)}(0)|\ge j!\rho^j$, where $j\ge1$ and
$0<\vartheta=\rho R/8<1$, then, for
$\kappa=16[1+\log(1/\vartheta)+\log(8/3)]$,
$$
\|g\|_{[0,R/4]}\ge
\frac1{8\kappa}\left(\frac{\vartheta}{8e^2\kappa^2}\right)^j.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-transfer}
:::

[]{#proof-nth-storage-analytic-transfer}

::: {.proof}
For a degree-$N$ polynomial $P$, map $[0,R/4]$ to $[-1,1]$.
Its nonconstant Chebyshev coefficients have modulus at most $2\|P\|$,
by their cosine integral formula, and
$$
|T_k^{(j)}(-1)|=\prod_{r=0}^{j-1}\frac{k^2-r^2}{2r+1}
\le k^{2j}/j!,\qquad
|P^{(j)}(0)|\le\frac{2N}{j!}(8N^2/R)^j\|P\|_{[0,R/4]}.
$$
For $k<j$ the derivative is zero; for $k\ge j$ the product formula follows
by successively differentiating
$(1-x^2)T_k''-xT_k'+k^2T_k=0$ at $x=-1$.
Take the degree-$N=\lceil\kappa j\rceil$ Taylor polynomial of $g$.
Cauchy's coefficient bound gives remainder at most $(2/3)4^{-N}$.
Since its $j$th derivative agrees with that of $g$,
$$
\|g\|_{[0,R/4]}\ge
\frac{\vartheta^j(j!)^2}{2N^{2j+1}}-\frac23\,4^{-N}.
$$
To verify that the tail is at most half the first term, put
$u=\log(1/\vartheta)$, $v=\log(8/3)$, $D=1+u+v$.
Using $N\le2\kappa j$, $\log(j!)\ge j\log j-j$, and $\log j\le j$,
$$
ju+(2j+1)\log N-2\log(j!)+v
\le j[u+v+3\log(2\kappa)+3]
\le15jD<\kappa j\log4\le N\log4.
$$
The second inequality uses $\kappa=16D$, $\log32<4$ and
$\log D\le D-1$. Exponentiation proves the tail comparison.
The resulting lower bound
$\vartheta^j(j!)^2/(4N^{2j+1})$, with the same factorial bound,
$N\le2\kappa j$ and $j\le2^j$, yields @eq-nth-storage-transfer.
:::

::: {#lem-nth-storage-dense-small-ball}
### An actual dense-pair lower bound

For every fixed deterministic dataset in the setup with $n\ge4$,
$1\le d\le n$, and $b\ne0$,
with probability at least $1-4e/\sqrt n-4e^{-c_*n}$,
$$
D_n\ge\frac{\|b\|_2}{2^{31}n^2}.
$$ {#eq-nth-storage-dense-lower}
:::

[]{#proof-nth-storage-dense-small-ball}

::: {.proof}
Use $v_*=b/\|b\|_2$ and $g(t)=f_n(t,v_*)-\widetilde f_n(t,v_*)$.
On the pair's matrix-norm event, @lem-nth-storage-source-control bounds
$|g|\le2\|b\|_2$ on $|t|<R_0$.
Set $R=2^{-13}$, so $T=R/4$.
For $0\le t\le T$ the radius-$R/2$ circle centered at $t$ lies in this
disk; Cauchy's formula gives $|g''(t)|\le2^{30}\|b\|_2$.
At initialization,
$$
f_n'(0,v_*)=\|b\|_2 H,\qquad
H=\|W_0B_0v_*\|_2^2\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\ UV,
$$
where $U,V$ are independent $\chi_n^2/n$ variables.
Indeed $U=\|B_0v_*\|_2^2$, and conditional on $B_0v_*$ the ratio
$H/U$ has that same chi-square law independently of the conditioning vector.

For $n\ge4$, the density $p(u)=C_nu^{n/2-1}e^{-nu/2}$ is maximal at
$u_0=1-2/n\ge1/2$. On $[u_0,u_0+n^{-1/2}]$ its logarithm has zero
initial derivative and second derivative at least $-2n$.
Thus $p(u)\ge e^{-1}p(u_0)$ there and $\|p\|_\infty\le e\sqrt n$.
Integration by parts in the same density gives
$\mathbb E V^{-1}=n/(n-2)\le2$.
The product density satisfies $\|p_H\|_\infty\le2e\sqrt n$,
and convolution gives the same bound for $H-\widetilde H$.
Therefore $\Pr(|H-\widetilde H|\le a)\le4e\sqrt n\,a$.
Taking $a=1/n$ gives $|g'(0)|\ge\|b\|_2/n$ outside an event of
probability $4e/\sqrt n$, without conditioning on the matrix norms.
Intersect afterward with their good event.
At $t_n=1/(2^{30}n)\le T$, Taylor's integral remainder now gives
$|g(t_n)|\ge\|b\|_2/(2^{31}n^2)$, proving the assertion.
:::

[]{#proof-nth-storage-main}

::: {.proof}
For the general upper, combine @eq-nth-storage-geometric and
@eq-nth-storage-dense-lower to get
$E_n(q)/D_n\le2^{37}n^2\,1024^{-q}$ when $b\ne0$.
The choice @eq-nth-storage-order proves
@cor-nth-storage-general-upper, including its probability.
For $b=0$, uniqueness gives the claimed exact zero predictions instead.
The counts follow by summing @eq-nth-storage-counts.

For the lower, apply @lem-nth-storage-analytic-transfer to $g_q$ from
@lem-nth-storage-omitted-derivative with
$R=2^{-13}$ and $\rho=Y/64$; the common analytic bound is two.
Since $g_q=\bar v^\top(w-w_q)$ and $\lambda\le1$, $E_n(q)\ge\|g_q\|_{[0,T]}$.
Writing
$$
\kappa_Y=16[1+\log(2^{22}/Y)+\log(8/3)],\qquad
a_Y=(8\kappa_Y)^{-1},\qquad
b_Y=\log(2^{25}e^2\kappa_Y^2/Y),
$$
gives, on one event of probability $1-Ce^{-cn}$,
$E_n(q)\ge a_Ye^{-b_Yj}$ simultaneously for every $q\ge2$.
Put $R_n=n/(m+\log(en))$.
If $q\le(4b_Y)^{-1}\log R_n$, then $j\le q+1$ gives
$E_n(q)\ge a_Ye^{-b_Y}R_n^{-1/4}$, whereas
@eq-nth-storage-dense-upper gives $D_n\le C R_n^{-1/2}$.
Because $R_n\to\infty$ uniformly in $4\le m\le\sqrt n$, these bounds imply
$E_n(q)>A D_n$ simultaneously over these orders. Thus their success probability
for any fixed factor $A$ tends to zero, and eventually is below $p$.

Literal training arrays alone have at least $m^{q-1}$ entries, even after
omitting a zero odd top; nonfrozen arrays have at least $m^{q-2}$.
The necessary order therefore costs
$\exp[c_Y\log m\log R_n]$ in either convention.
Uniformly in the sample range $\log R_n$ is bounded above and below by
positive absolute multiples of $\log n$ for sufficiently large $n$.
For the upper, $q_n=O(\log n)$ has success tending to one and error
at most $D_n/n$. With $d=m+1$, its count is at most $5m^{q_n}+md+m$.
These prove @thm-nth-storage-matching and its moving-array assertion.
For an adaptive order under a deterministic smaller budget, every permitted
order lies in the simultaneously excluded range, proving the stated
budget interpretation.
:::

The matched result concerns a growing-data, deep-linear model, a specified
literal tensor representation, and the window $[0,2^{-15}]$ in half-MSE
physical time. All layers are trainable, but the input-output function is
linear. No longer-time, nonlinear-activation, arbitrary-encoding, or
finite-precision conclusion is asserted. Fixed $m,d$ give polynomial size;
the superpolynomial example grows $m$ and $d$ together with width.
Here $Y$ is fixed independently of $m,n$. The fixed-data small-label
hypotheses of the complete-trajectory compression theorem are therefore
not assumptions of this result. Its fitting and dense-variability theorems
are not used, and this result establishes no same-family storage separation
from those compression constructions.

## 6. Scope and obstructions to stronger calculus claims {#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1749}

**No full same-norm product closure with an unbounded atom.** Let
$\mathfrak X$ be a normed space of random variables containing an
essentially unbounded $X$ and all its powers. Suppose, for fixed
$1\le p<\infty$ and $A,C>0$,
$\|V\|_{L^p}\le A\|V\|_{\mathfrak X}$ and
$\|UV\|_{\mathfrak X}\le C\|U\|_{\mathfrak X}\|V\|_{\mathfrak X}$.
Iteration and the identity
$\|X^k\|_{L^p}=\|X\|_{L^{kp}}^k$ give

$$
 \|X\|_{L^{kp}}
 \le A^{1/k}C^{1-1/k}\|X\|_{\mathfrak X}.              
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1759}

The right side is bounded. For any $B>0$, essential unboundedness gives
$\mathbb P(|X|>B)>0$, and
$\|X\|_{L^q}\ge B\,\mathbb P(|X|>B)^{1/q}$.
Letting $q\to\infty$, then $B\to\infty$, contradicts ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1759]).
In particular a nondegenerate Gaussian atom cannot belong to such a full same-space
algebra. For a derivative-sum norm containing constants, the zero-order
weight must be positive; if its exponent is finite it supplies the
embedding used here, and if it is infinity it already excludes the
unbounded atom. This obstruction does not apply to the finite,
order-consuming moment estimates of [Section 5](02-gaussian-reuse.qmd#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l263).

**Independent coefficientwise jet obstruction.** On the unrestricted
space of finitely supported ordinary-derivative jets
$u=(u_j)_{j\ge0}$, let
$\|u\|_w=\sum_{j\ge0}w_j|u_j|$, with every $w_j>0$.
Suppose both the shift $(Su)_j=u_{j+1}$ and the Leibniz product
$(u\star v)_j=\sum_{i=0}^j\binom ji u_i v_{j-i}$
have fixed bounds $C_S$ and $C_P$ in this same norm.
Testing the shift on the unit jet $e_j$, and the product on
$e_1,e_{j-1}$, gives, for every $j\ge2$,

$$
 w_{j-1}\le C_Sw_j,\qquad
 j w_j\le C_Pw_1w_{j-1},\qquad
 j\le C_PC_Sw_1,                                     
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1783}

which is impossible. For factorial-normalized derivatives the product
loses its binomial factor but the shift becomes
$(Su)_j=(j+1)u_{j+1}$; the same tests again give ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1783])'s final
contradiction. This statement concerns unrestricted positive
coefficientwise majorants, not an arbitrary restricted class of
expressions with cancellations.

**Zero Taylor radius does not exclude a smooth nonsingular ODE.** For
a standard Gaussian $G$, put $g(t)=\mathbb E(1+t^2G^2)^{-1}$.
Every derivative of $\psi(u)=(1+u^2)^{-1}$ is bounded on the real
line: repeated differentiation gives a rational function without a
real pole that tends to zero at infinity. The integrable bound
$|G|^j\|\psi^{(j)}\|_\infty$ therefore justifies every derivative
under the expectation, so $g\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$. At zero,

$$
 \frac{g^{(2k)}(0)}{(2k)!}
   =(-1)^k\mathbb E G^{2k}=(-1)^k(2k-1)!!,\qquad
 g^{(2k+1)}(0)=0.                                    
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1802}

The even derivative identity follows from the finite geometric expansion
of $(1+u^2)^{-1}$; the Gaussian moment recurrence follows by integration
by parts, as in [Section 4](02-gaussian-reuse.qmd#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l203). Consecutive nonzero Taylor terms at $t\ne0$
have absolute ratio $(2k+1)t^2$, so the Taylor series has radius zero.
Nevertheless the autonomous smooth system

$$
 \dot s=1,\qquad \dot q=g'(s),\qquad s(0)=0,\quad q(0)=1
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l1812}

has the exact solution $s(t)=t,\ q(t)=g(t)$; integration of the two
equations also proves uniqueness. Its vector field never vanishes,
because its first component is one. Here $s,q$ are auxiliary scalar
ODE coordinates, not network feature time or backward fields.
Thus failure of analyticity alone is not an obstruction to a smooth
finite-dimensional realization. Conversely, this example does not
supply a network closure, a convergent flow Taylor series, or a
depth- or time-uniform extension of the fixed-program theorem.

## 7.2. A quadratic initialization-jet certificate {#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2156}

The following is a reusable, finite algebraic part of the calculus. It is
not a claim that a high-order compiler, an infinite Taylor series, or a
positive-time population evolution has been verified. The implementation
`pde.exact_calculus` supplies a canonical forest key, rational finite-series
reversion, rational determinants, and one completely specified certificate.
No retained table is an input to these operations. The [decorated-forest factorization and canonical keys](02-gaussian-reuse.qmd#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2165) are developed in the MFP chapter.

### A fully specified quadratic initialization-jet obstruction {#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2248}

This example uses a different metric and initialization from the main
nonlinear training theorem. It is a negative test of a proposed universal
representation, not a recommended model for feature learning. There is one
sample $x=y=1$, $d=1$, $L=2$, quadratic activations, and

$$
 W^{(1)}_j=u_j,\quad W^{(2)}_{ij}=g_{ij}/\sqrt n,
 \quad W^{(3)}_i=a_i,\qquad
 z_i^{(2)}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_j g_{ij}u_j^2,
 \quad f_n=\frac1n\sum_i a_i(z_i^{(2)})^2.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2254}

All the displayed initialization Gaussians are independent standard normals;
the stored readout is order one. Freeze only the first parameter block and
use feature ascent, with hidden stored-block mobility one and readout
mobility $n$. Thus, in the auxiliary unscaled matrix coordinates,

$$
 \frac{da_i}{ds}=(z_i^{(2)})^2,\qquad
 \frac{dg_{ij}}{ds}=\frac2{\sqrt n}a_i z_i^{(2)}u_j^2,
 \qquad \frac{du_j}{ds}=0.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2265}

These equations follow by differentiating ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2254]); they are not loss GD or
physical-time GF. Put $q_n=n^{-1}\sum_j u_j^4$. Differentiating the
preactivation gives $dz_i^{(2)}/ds=2q_n a_i z_i^{(2)}$. Therefore the
exact finite initialization derivative of order $k$ is

$$
 \left.\frac{d^k f_n}{ds^k}\right|_{s=0}
 =\frac1n\sum_i \mathscr D_{q_n}^{k}(a_i(z_i^{(2)})^2),
 \quad \mathscr D_q=z^2\partial_a+2qaz\partial_z.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2275}

Here $a,z$ are the two scalar arguments of a polynomial; the superscript
on $\mathscr D$ is repeated application, not a weight-layer index.
Repeated chain rule proves ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2275]), since $q_n$ is constant along ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2265]).
Smooth finite equations have a local solution at every initial state; no
positive-time uniform existence is needed to define these derivatives.

Conditional on all $u_j$, the pairs $(a_i,z_i^{(2)})$ at initialization
are independent, with laws $N(0,1)\otimes N(0,q_n)$. Set
$z=\sqrt q\,\xi$. Then
$\mathscr D_q=q(\xi^2\partial_a+2a\xi\partial_\xi)$ and
$az^2=qa\xi^2$. Conditional expectation of ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2275]) is consequently
$c_k q_n^{k+1}$, for a fixed finite constant $c_k$.

To pass to the unconditional limit without a probabilistic black box, note
that $E u^4=3$ and independence imply $E(q_n-3)^2=\operatorname{Var}(u^4)/n$.
For every positive integer $b$, convexity gives
$E q_n^{2b}\le E|u|^{8b}<\infty$, uniformly in $n$.
For a nonnegative $x$, factorization of $x^b-3^b$ bounds its absolute
value by $b|x-3|\max(x,3)^{b-1}$. Cauchy--Schwarz and the preceding
moment bound show $E|q_n^b-3^b|\to0$. Hence all fixed-order annealed
initialization derivatives have the exact limit

$$
 d_k=E\mathscr D^k(AZ^2),\qquad
 \mathscr D=z^2\partial_a+6az\partial_z,\quad
 A\sim N(0,1),\ Z\sim N(0,3)\text{ independent}.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2302}

The expectation is of the polynomial after substitution $(a,z)=(A,Z)$.
This proves the probabilistic interpretation of this particular coefficient
recurrence. It does not interchange an infinite series with a width limit.

The elementary monomial rules are

$$
 \mathscr D(a^p z^q)=p a^{p-1}z^{q+2}+6q a^{p+1}z^q,
 \qquad E[A^pZ^q]=
 \begin{cases}(p-1)!!(q-1)!!3^{q/2},&p,q\text{ even},\\0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2313}

Use $(-1)!!=1$. The moment rule follows by integrating the Gaussian
density derivative by parts, starting with moment zero equal to one;
independence multiplies the two moments. Each application changes the
parity of the $a$ exponent and preserves the parity of the $z$ exponent.
Thus all even $d_k$ vanish. Starting from the single monomial $az^2$,
([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2313]) through order thirteen gives

$$
 (d_1,d_3,d_5,d_7,d_9,d_{11},d_{13})=
 (63,77760,274547232,2141006515200,31149221916487680,
 759035131220036321280,28719223368439752070594560).
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2326}

For instance the first differentiated polynomial is $z^4+12a^2z^2$,
whose expectation is $27+36=63$. The finite recurrence ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2313]), not a
table read from another source, specifies every other integer in ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2326]).

Form the formal series $F(s)=\sum_{k\ge0}d_k s^k/k!$. This is a
formal algebraic object; no convergence is presumed. Its zero constant and
nonzero linear coefficient give a unique formal inverse $B(y)$.
Define $K(y)=F'(B(y))$. Since $F$ is odd, uniqueness makes $B$
odd and $K$ even. Define the coefficients $\mu_j$ by

$$
 K(y)=63+y^2\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^j\mu_j y^{2j}.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2341}

Only ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2326]) is needed for $\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_5$. There is no use
of a specialized inversion theorem: if $a_k=d_k/k!$, let $b_0=0$,
$b_1=1/a_1$, and successively set

$$
 b_k=-\frac1{a_1}[y^k]\sum_{j=2}^k a_j
                  \left(\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}b_i y^i\right)^j.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2348}

The only degree-$k$ term involving the unknown $b_k$ in $F(B(y))$
is $a_1b_k$; thus induction proves both existence and uniqueness and
the formula. Ordinary convolution gives each product coefficient.
Substitution in $F'(B(y))$ gives exactly

$$
 (\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_5)=\left(
 \frac{480}{49},\frac{43756}{151263},\frac{7214528}{200120949},
 \frac{12545175968}{2402451992745},
 \frac{171752915595136}{200241971143303005},
 \frac{2199776554157960896}{14570607030242443158825}\right).
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2357}

These six coefficients cannot be moments of a nonnegative measure on
$[0,\infty)$. Indeed the shifted moment matrix
$M_{ij}=\mu_{i+j+1}$, $0\le i,j\le2$, satisfies

$$
 \det M=-\frac{86245462994269879146938487857152}
 {200150589172828762588730609071155193161975}<0.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2369}

There is also a direct polynomial witness, avoiding a definiteness criterion.
Let $p(\lambda)=v_0+v_1\lambda+\lambda^2$, where

$$
 v_0=\frac{40042013405871059816}{2310453239160606810795},\qquad
 v_1=-\frac{14165989123115588}{49896409440894219}.
$$

Direct rational multiplication of ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2357]) gives

$$
 \sum_{i,j=0}^2v_i v_j\mu_{i+j+1}
 =-\frac{673792679642733430835456936384}
 {329714727520793070279653295504327135}<0,
 \qquad v_2=1.
$$ {#eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2381}

If such a representing measure $\nu$ existed, this finite sum would
equal $\int\lambda p(\lambda)^2\nu(d\lambda)\ge0$. This is the
contradiction. All relevant moments are finite by the representation being
tested. The result refutes a representation demanded uniformly over metrics
including this zero first-block mobility. It does not settle the unit-metric
case, any strictly positive first mobility, or an actual positive-time
population equation. Nonexistence of this moment representation is not
nonexistence of a nonlinear feature-learning limit.

### Implementation and independent checking routes {#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2397}

$\mathrm{revert\_series}$ accepts ordinary rational coefficients and implements ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2348])
by truncated composition in Horner order. Multiplication is the finite
convolution $(ab)_k=\sum_{i=0}^k a_i b_{k-i}$. It returns all inverse
coefficients to the same length, without mutating its input. A nonzero
constant or zero linear coefficient is rejected. $\mathrm{determinant}$ eliminates
successive columns using a nonzero pivot, swapping rows when necessary and
tracking the determinant sign. Subtracting multiples of one row from another
preserves the determinant; each pivot multiplies the remaining triangular
determinant. If no pivot exists, the remaining first column is zero and the
determinant is zero. The empty determinant is one. This proves its algorithm
over the rational field, including singular matrices.

`quadratic_axis_certificate()` generates ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2326]) directly from ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2313]), reverts
the ordinary series using ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2348]), composes its derivative to produce ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2357]),
and constructs the witness by solving the leading two-by-two shifted system:

$$
 v_0=\frac{\mu_2\mu_4-\mu_3^2}{\mu_1\mu_3-\mu_2^2},\qquad
 v_1=\frac{\mu_2\mu_3-\mu_1\mu_4}{\mu_1\mu_3-\mu_2^2}.
$$

The positive denominator is checked before division. Tests independently
compare the six displayed fractions and evaluate ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2381]) from the displayed
witness; a Leibniz-permutation determinant checks the elimination route.
Series tests compose both directions of reversion, and forest tests check
relabelling, edge order, component multiplicity, invalid graphs and changed
decorations. They do not validate an unimplemented general-depth generator.

All scalar arithmetic in this module is integer or $\mathrm{fractions.Fraction}$;
floating values and booleans are rejected by its rational interfaces.
Graph indices and colors are nonnegative Python integers, with layer one or
two. Inputs are finite lists or tuples. Results are freshly constructed;
there is no cross-call cache, sampling or file output. Rational bit sizes and
the all-roots tree-key cost can grow, so these are small transparent reference
primitives, not performance claims for large-order campaigns. Python recursion
limits still apply to the recursive tree key.

The established unit-test command in the code guide regenerates all displayed
coefficient and witness checks. No generated data, historical coefficient
array, symbolic package or external source is required. Exact arithmetic
certifies these finite computations, while ([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2254])--([-@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l2313]) supply the separate
initialization-jet interpretation. Neither part supplies a positive-time
identification bridge.
